newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss government welcomes call for Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss government welcomes call for Holocaust fund.

text.p: The Swiss government on Thursday welcomed a top banker's unexpected call for a Holocaust memorial fund as a gesture of goodwill to Jewish critics of Switzerland's financial role in World War Two.
The Federal Council, or cabinet, said it would talk with banks about setting up a fund to compensate impoverished survivors of Nazi persecution or their heirs.

"As announced before on January 7, the Federal Council is prepared to continue the necessary talks with all interested parties, especially in order to clarify the form and mandate of a fund," a cabinet statement said.
"In this connection, the council welcomes the willingness of various banking circles to move quickly on getting a fund started," the statement added.

This refered to a call by Rainer Gut, chairman of banking conglomerate Credit Suisse Group, for a bold move to repair Switzerland's reputation from allegations it bankrolled Nazi Germany and hoarded the wealth of Holocaust victims.
Gut said the fund would have to be much larger than 100 million Swiss francs ($70 million).

His comments were the first by the head of one of the Swiss "Big Three" global banks -- Credit Suisse, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- to indicate they were leaning towards rapid payment as a gesture of remorse.

The big banks' efforts to expand their lucrative international business are threatened by damage to Switzerland's world standing from an ongoing dispute with groups led by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) over the fate of money left by Holocaust victims.

The cabinet said on January 7 it was willing to start talks with banks and Jewish groups about a Holocaust memorial fund. The latest statement indicated it was leaning towards a shared payment by the banks and by government.

"A decision on a potential federal government role in financing the fund will be made when hardened historical facts are presented," the cabinet said in reference to a panel of historians it appointed in December.
The nine Swiss and international historians, headed by Zurich professor Jean-Francois Bergier, are charged with clarifying a broad range of allegations that the Swiss profited cynically from the war.

Bergier said first conclusions -- which could form the basis for a cabinet decision to pay into a Holocaust fund -- were due as early as mid-1997 in the form of provisional reports on the first two topic under research.

These topics are Swiss national bank purchases of Nazi gold stolen from German-occupied countries and Holocaust victims and Swiss refugee policy that turned back thousands of Jews to face near-certain death in Nazi camps.
"I told the Federal Council we would look into these subjects first, as it requested," Bergier told Reuters.

The Bergier commission's job will be to assemble the scattered facts on both issues, which have been fairly well researched, and present them in a clear fashion to the cabinet for a decision on the political consequences. ($1=1.4260 Swiss Franc)
